title: Seed stitch
subtitle: Small paired straight stitches scattered at random angles to build light texture and shading
excerpt: Seed stitch is a filling stitch made from tiny paired straight stitches placed at varying angles across a shape. The stitches sit close together or spread out to control the density of texture. By changing thread colour or stitch density, seed stitch can suggest shading and soft texture in a natural, unstructured way.
sourceNotes: Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), flat and filling stitches sections (Project Gutenberg #20776). Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882).

content.text: Seed stitch is a scattered filling stitch from the flat stitch family. Each seed is a pair of tiny straight stitches placed side by side, and the pairs are scattered at different angles across a shape to build texture. The stitches neither line up in rows nor radiate from a centre; the random placement is what gives the filling its soft, natural quality. It is used for backgrounds, the bodies of flowers and leaves, and any area where a light, airy texture is needed rather than a solid fill.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton, 1 or 2 strands for fine texture; 2 or 3 strands for a heavier fill

content.text: Secure the thread on the back and bring the needle up at point A anywhere inside the shape.
Insert the needle down at point B, 2 to 3 mm away in any direction. This is the first stitch of the pair. Come back up at point C, immediately beside point A (about 1 mm away).

Insert the needle down at point D, parallel to AB and immediately beside it. This completes one seed: a pair of tiny parallel stitches. The two stitches of each seed should be close enough to look like a single short mark at a glance.

Move to a new position in the shape and work the next pair at a different angle, turning the direction roughly 45 to 90 degrees from the last pair. Continue scattering pairs at varying angles until the shape is filled to the density you want.

For a shaded effect, place the pairs more densely at the darker end of the shape and more sparsely towards the lighter edge. A second pass in a lighter or darker thread can then fill the gaps to blend the tones. When the shape is complete, fasten off on the back.

items.symptom: The filling looks stripy or regimented rather than scattered
items.cause: The pairs are all pointing the same way or placed in tidy rows
items.fix: After every pair, consciously change direction. Think of the pairs as scattered at random: some horizontal, some vertical, some diagonal. Avoid drifting into a grid.

items.symptom: The filling looks patchy with obvious gaps and clumps
items.cause: Working from one side of the shape to the other rather than spreading evenly
items.fix: Place a few seeds across the whole shape first to establish density, then fill in the gaps. This distributes them more evenly than working row by row.

content.text: Seed stitch is used as a light filling in crewelwork and surface embroidery, for backgrounds, flower petals and anywhere a breathable texture is preferred over a solid fill. The individual seeds are single
